common_name: Zebrina Mallow (French Hollyhock, Striped-Flower Ornamental Mallow)

planting.note: Direct-sow in cool spring or fall in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; Zebrina is the classic striped-flower selection of common mallow long grown as a cottage-garden ornamental.

directions: Zebrina bears the same edible young leaves, stems, and 'cheeses' (round seed pods) as ordinary common mallow, but is grown chiefly for its striking flowers — pale lilac-white petals boldly veined and streaked with deep violet-purple, giving each bloom a distinctive candy-striped appearance that has made it a fixture of English cottage borders for generations and earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Direct-sow into well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; like the species, Zebrina tolerates poor soil and drought once established but produces the most abundant bloom with regular moisture through summer. Plants form an upright, branching clump 3-4 feet tall that flowers continuously from early summer into fall, and readily self-seeds true to type in favorable conditions, though scattered seedlings sometimes revert toward plain pink species flowers. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering and reduce unwanted self-sowing where a tidier planting is wanted.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector (Malva sylvestris 'Zebrina')
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
Plants For a Future (PFAF)

common_name: Martini Manuka (Compact Double-Pink New Zealand Tea Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean sandy or gritty soil in full sun; Martini is a compact double-flowered manuka cultivar propagated only from semi-hardwood cuttings, since it does not come true from seed.

directions: Martini is a compact, densely branched manuka selection prized for smothering itself in small, fully double, soft-pink flowers over a long late-winter-into-spring bloom season, with a tidier, more restrained habit than the species that makes it well suited to smaller borders, large containers, and rock gardens rather than the open shrubbery manuka typically forms. Plant in lean, gritty, slightly acidic soil with excellent drainage in full sun; like all Leptospermum, it is markedly more tolerant of drought and poor soil than of wet feet, and root rot in heavy or poorly drained ground is the most common cause of failure. Because the fully double flowers produce little accessible nectar or pollen, Martini offers less value to foraging bees than single-flowered manuka, so gardeners wanting both ornament and pollinator value should pair it with species plants or other single-flowered cultivars nearby. Trim lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, compact form.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector
New Zealand Plant Conservation Network
Monrovia — Leptospermum scoparium cultivar descriptions

common_name: Red Damask Manuka (Classic Double Dark-Red New Zealand Tea Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean soil in full sun; Red Damask is one of the oldest and most widely distributed double-flowered manuka cultivars and is propagated from semi-hardwood cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Red Damask is a long-established, vigorous manuka cultivar covered in late winter through spring with masses of small, fully double, deep crimson-red flowers that give the whole shrub a rich, dark-red glow from a distance — a dramatic contrast to the white flowers of the wild species. It grows larger and more upright than many newer compact manuka selections, making a substantial evergreen accent or informal hedge in mild-winter gardens. Grow in lean, gritty, slightly acidic soil with sharp drainage in full sun; the fine, heather-like foliage and tolerance of coastal wind and salt spray make it a reliable choice for exposed sites, but it will not tolerate waterlogged soil. Like other double-flowered manuka cultivars, its dense, ruffled flowers offer bees far less accessible nectar than the species, so plant it as an ornamental accent rather than a bee-forage shrub.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector
New Zealand Plant Conservation Network
Palmers Garden Centres (NZ) — Leptospermum cultivar guide

common_name: Crimson Glory Manuka (Double Maroon-Red New Zealand Tea Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean soil in full sun; Crimson Glory is a double-flowered manuka cultivar with dark maroon-red blooms, propagated from semi-hardwood cuttings.

directions: Crimson Glory produces densely packed, fully double flowers in a deep, dusky maroon-red that reads almost purple in certain light, one of the darkest flower colors available among manuka cultivars and a striking companion to the pinks and reds of other Leptospermum selections in a mixed shrub border. Foliage is the typical tiny, needle-like, aromatic manuka leaf on an upright, medium-sized evergreen shrub. Grow in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; manuka cultivars are markedly more drought-tolerant than moisture-tolerant, and root rot in heavy, poorly drained soil is the leading cause of decline. Light shearing after the spring flush keeps the shrub dense and well-shaped; avoid hard pruning into old bare wood, from which manuka regenerates poorly.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector
New Zealand Plant Conservation Network

common_name: Heidekind Veronica (Compact Rose-Pink Spike Speedwell)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Heidekind is a compact, German-bred spiked speedwell cultivar valued for its dense rose-pink flower spikes and low, tidy habit.

directions: Heidekind ('Heath Child') is a dwarf, mat-forming selection of spiked speedwell that produces dense, tapering spikes of intense rose-pink flowers held just above a low mound of gray-green foliage, blooming from early summer into fall with deadheading. Its compact 8-12 inch height makes it one of the shortest Veronica spicata cultivars in general cultivation, ideal for the front of a sunny border, rock garden, or edging where taller spike speedwells would overwhelm neighboring plants. Plant in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; like the species it declines in rich, overly moist ground where it becomes floppy and short-lived, performing best in lean conditions that keep growth compact and tight. Shear back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage a strong second flowering later in the season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: White Wood Betony (Alba Wood Betony)

planting.note: Sow seed or plant divisions in early spring in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Alba is the white-flowered form of wood betony, otherwise identical to the species in habit and history.

directions: Alba is the white-flowered selection of wood betony, forming the same neat rosettes of deeply veined, scallop-edged, dark-green foliage as the species but topped in early summer by upright spikes of clean white tubular flowers instead of the typical rose-pink to magenta of the type plant. It brightens a partly shaded herb garden or woodland-edge planting and combines especially well with darker-flowered companions, where its pale spikes read as a cooling accent rather than competing with the species' hot pink tones. Grow exactly as the species: moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, undemanding once established, and long-lived without division. Bumblebees and other long-tongued pollinators visit the white form as readily as the pink, making it a useful addition to a wildlife or medicinal herb border without sacrificing pollinator value for color variety.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector
Jelitto Perennial Seeds — Stachys officinalis cultivar list
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

common_name: Prince Rupert Lemon Geranium (Vigorous Upright Scented Pelargonium)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens after frost in well-drained, average potting mix or garden soil in partial shade to full sun; Prince Rupert is a vigorous, larger-growing, strongly lemon-scented selection of lemon geranium, one of the oldest named scented pelargonium cultivars still in cultivation.

directions: Prince Rupert is a historic, strong-growing lemon geranium cultivar dating to the eighteenth century, distinguished from the species by larger, more coarsely crinkled leaves and a more vigorous, upright habit that quickly fills out into a substantial sub-shrub. The crushed foliage releases the same clean, true lemon fragrance prized in lemon geranium generally, used to flavor sugars, cakes, and teas, but Prince Rupert's bigger leaves make for faster, more generous harvests than the species type. Root stem cuttings in a well-drained mix or plant container specimens in partial shade to full sun; it tolerates a bit more shade than most pelargoniums but flowers and grows most vigorously with several hours of direct sun. In zones 9-11 it persists outdoors as a woody perennial; elsewhere grow it in a container and bring it indoors to a bright window before frost, pinching regularly to keep its vigorous growth in a manageable, bushy form.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector
Geraniaceae Group — Pelargonium crispum cultivars

common_name: French Lace Lemon Geranium (Cream-Variegated Compact Scented Pelargonium)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens after frost in well-drained, average potting mix in partial shade to full sun; French Lace is a compact, cream-margined variegated sport of lemon geranium grown as much for its foliage color as for its lemon scent.

directions: French Lace pairs the same crinkled, fan-shaped, lemon-scented foliage typical of lemon geranium with a striking creamy-white leaf margin that gives the small, dense plant an eye-catching, frosted look even when not in bloom, making it as much a foliage accent for mixed containers as a culinary herb. Its more compact, restrained growth compared to larger green-leaved lemon geranium cultivars suits it well to smaller pots, window boxes, and the front of an herb garden bed. Root stem cuttings in a well-drained mix and grow in partial shade to full sun; variegated pelargoniums generally hold their leaf pattern best with a little protection from the most intense midday sun, which can scorch the pale leaf margins. In zones 9-11 grow as a perennial sub-shrub outdoors; elsewhere overwinter as a container plant in a bright, cool indoor spot, watering sparingly through winter dormancy.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector

common_name: Purple Wild Angelica (Vicar's Mead)

planting.note: Direct-sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in fall in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Purpurea' (also sold as 'Vicar's Mead') is the deep-purple-stemmed ornamental selection of wild angelica prized in naturalistic garden design.

directions: 'Purpurea', distributed in the nursery trade as both 'Purpurea' and 'Vicar's Mead' (the two names refer to the same selection), intensifies the purplish stem tinting of the wild species into deep, glossy purple-black stems and leaf ribs that persist through the whole plant, topped by the same rounded umbels of white to pink-flushed flowers in summer. The striking dark stems have made it a favorite of naturalistic and 'new perennial' style planting design, where its architectural height and moody coloring pair well against airy grasses and pale-flowered companions in a damp, partly shaded border. Sow fresh seed in fall — viability drops quickly in storage — in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil at a woodland edge, streamside bed, or other consistently damp, partly shaded site. Like the species it is monocarpic, dying after flowering and setting seed in its second or third year, but self-sows reliably enough to maintain a colony of purple-stemmed plants once established, provided at least some seedlings are allowed to mature and set seed each cycle.
sources: Great Dixter Nursery — Angelica sylvestris 'Vicar's Mead'
Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector

common_name: Parabinga Barrel Medic

planting.note: Direct sow in fall with fresh medic-specific Rhizobium inoculant onto a firm, well-drained, alkaline-to-neutral seedbed; Parabinga is an older, broadly-adapted Australian barrel medic cultivar and one of the founding cultivars against which newer barrel medic releases such as 'Caliph' and 'Paraggio' are routinely compared in regional trials.

directions: Broadcast 'Parabinga' onto a firm, well-drained, alkaline-to-neutral seedbed in early fall, inoculating fresh seed with medic-specific Rhizobium if the field has no recent medic-growing history. Released in Australia and long grown across Mediterranean-climate pasture and cropping regions, Parabinga is a mid-season-maturing barrel medic valued for broad soil adaptability and reliable pod and seed set, though newer cultivars bred specifically for higher seed yield, such as 'Caliph', have outperformed it in some regional variety trials. Its low, spreading annual growth fixes nitrogen for the following crop while its small, spiny, coiled pods build a persistent hard-seed bank in the soil that supports self-regeneration in subsequent autumns without replanting. Terminate by grazing, mowing, or light tillage once a good proportion of pods have matured and set seed, leaving enough hard seed in the ground to carry the stand into the next growing season.
sources: South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI) — Pasture Legume Variety Guide
NSW Department of Primary Industries — Barrel Medic
UC SAREP Cover Crop Database — Barrel Medic

common_name: Paros Yellow Serradella

planting.note: Sow direct in fall as temperatures cool, inoculating seed with an Ornithopus-specific Rhizobium strain; Paros is an older, more prostrate yellow serradella cultivar that the newer, more upright 'Charano' selection was specifically bred to improve upon for mechanical seed harvest.

directions: Broadcast Rhizobium-inoculated 'Paros' seed onto a firm, weed-free, sandy, acidic seedbed in fall; like all serradella it fails to nodulate without an Ornithopus-specific inoculant strain, since common pasture-legume Rhizobium does not infect its roots. Paros is a lower-growing, more prostrate yellow serradella selection than newer upright cultivars such as 'Charano', spreading close to the ground in a dense mat that provides excellent early groundcover and weed suppression, though its sprawling habit makes standing pods harder to header-harvest for seed than upright types. It thrives on the same low-fertility, acidic, sandy soils where clovers and vetches struggle, fixing nitrogen and building organic matter through a mild winter and spring growing season before senescing with summer heat. Mow or graze before pod shatter if reseeding is unwanted, or allow pods to ripen and drop naturally in orchard, vineyard, or pasture-cropping systems for a self-renewing stand.
sources: Centre for Legumes in Mediterranean Agriculture, University of Western Australia — Pasture Legume Cultivars
NSW Department of Primary Industries — Yellow Serradella
Crop & Pasture Science — Prospects for diversifying temperate pasture systems with serradella

common_name: Canyon Prince Wild Rye (Dwarf Silver-Blue Giant Wildrye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in well-drained, dry to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Canyon Prince is a dwarf, intensely silver-blue-foliaged selection of giant wild rye originally collected on Santa Cruz Island and propagated vegetatively rather than grown from seed to preserve its foliage color.

directions: Canyon Prince is a compact, densely clumping selection of giant wild rye chosen for its dramatic, intensely silver-blue foliage — a far more vivid blue-gray than the species' typical blue-green — combined with a much smaller, tidier stature that fits ordinary garden borders and parking-strip plantings where the towering, 6-8 foot species would overwhelm the space. Discovered on Santa Cruz Island off the Southern California coast, it is propagated by division or container liners rather than seed to preserve the true blue foliage color and compact habit. Plant in well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun to light shade; once established it is extremely drought tolerant and goes summer-dormant in dry-summer Mediterranean climates, requiring little to no irrigation. Cut back dried foliage in late winter before new spring growth emerges to keep the clump looking fresh, and use it as a striking foliage-color accent, erosion-control groundcover on slopes, or dry-shade planting under oaks where few other ornamental grasses perform.
sources: Las Pilitas Nursery — Leymus condensatus 'Canyon Prince'
Calscape / California Native Plant Society
University of California Cooperative Extension

common_name: Mott Dwarf Napiergrass (Compact Elephant Grass)

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings (sections with 2-3 nodes) in moist soil after soil warms to 65F; Mott is a dwarf, leafier napiergrass selection released by the University of Florida for forage and biomass plots too small for full-sized napier grass.

directions: Mott is a dwarf napiergrass cultivar released by the University of Florida, selected from a natural dwarf mutant for a shorter, leafier, more digestible plant that stays roughly half the height of standard napier grass while retaining the species' extraordinary productivity. Plant stem cuttings 3-4 inches deep at 18-30 inch spacing in moist, fertile soil; establishment is rapid and Mott can be cut for forage or chop-and-drop mulch every 4-6 weeks during the growing season, regrowing vigorously from the root crown after each cutting. Its higher leaf-to-stem ratio than tall napier types makes it more palatable and nutritious as cut-and-carry livestock forage, while its lower stature makes it far more manageable in home-scale tropical gardens and food forests as a chop-and-drop biomass and mulch producer. In zone 9 and the Gulf Coast it dies back after the first hard frost but typically regrows from the crown the following spring unless soil temperatures drop well below freezing for an extended period; where it persists, monitor for spread since Pennisetum purpureum can naturalize in frost-free areas.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mott Elephant Grass
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
FAO Animal Production and Health Division — Pennisetum purpureum

common_name: Delaney Sainfoin

planting.note: Sow seed-in-pod in early spring on well-drained, calcareous soil; Delaney is a newer, multi-cut sainfoin release bred for stronger regrowth after cutting than the older 'Remont' cultivar it was developed to improve upon, and performs especially well under irrigation.

directions: Broadcast or drill 'Delaney' seed-in-pod at 25-40 lb per acre into a firm, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline, calcareous seedbed in early spring; like all sainfoin it performs poorly on acidic or heavy, poorly drained ground. Developed as an improved multi-cut successor to the older Montana-bred 'Remont' cultivar, Delaney was selected specifically for faster, stronger regrowth after cutting or grazing, giving it an advantage in irrigated hay and cover-crop systems in the Intermountain West and Northern Rockies where more than one harvest per season is wanted. Its deep taproot fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis, breaks up compacted subsoil, and produces tannin-containing, non-bloating forage of high palatability to livestock and excellent value to native pollinators during its long bloom period. Allow the stand to flower fully to maximize its value as bee forage, and cut for hay or terminate as a cover once the desired proportion of the crop has flowered and set seed.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Forage and Range Research Laboratory, Logan, Utah
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Onobrychis viciifolia
Montana State University Extension — Sainfoin Production

common_name: Sabine Illinois Bundleflower (Texas Forage and Wildlife Selection)

planting.note: Scarify seed and broadcast or drill in spring into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in full sun; Sabine was released by the USDA-NRCS Knox City Plant Materials Center in Texas and is adapted to warmer, longer-season conditions than the more northerly 'Reno' Germplasm selection it is often compared against.

directions: Sabine is a Texas-sourced Illinois bundleflower release selected by USDA-NRCS for vigorous forage yield, palatability, and warm-season persistence in the southern Great Plains and Gulf Coast prairie region, in contrast to the more cold-adapted, Kansas-sourced 'Reno' Germplasm bred for the Central Plains. Scarify hard seed before planting to improve germination, then broadcast or drill into a firm, well-drained seedbed in full sun after the soil has warmed. The fine, fern-like, mimosa-type foliage and small white puffball flowers give way to distinctive coiled, bristly seed clusters that are heavily used by upland game birds, songbirds, and small mammals through fall and winter, making Sabine a favored component of wildlife food plots and rangeland reseeding mixes as well as a nitrogen-fixing forage legume for cattle. As a deep-rooted perennial it establishes slowly in its first season but persists for many years once established, improving soil nitrogen and organic matter without annual replanting.
sources: USDA NRCS Knox City Plant Materials Center, Texas
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Illinois Bundleflower
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Native Legume Forages

common_name: Molokai Purple Sweet Potato

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic sandy soil in full sun; Molokai Purple is a Hawaiian-origin heirloom distributed by small specialty growers alongside other named purple types such as All Purple and Purple Passion.

directions: Molokai Purple is a Hawaiian-origin heirloom sweet potato named for the island of Molokai, producing roots with dark purple to nearly black skin over dense, vividly purple flesh that holds its color well through baking and steaming. The vines are vigorous and trailing with purple-tinged foliage, and the roots are somewhat smaller and more irregular in shape than mainstream commercial purple varieties, reflecting its heirloom, unselected background. Set slips in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping fertility moderate since rich soil favors vine growth over root development; the vine tolerates the heat and humidity of a long warm season well. Harvest once vines begin to yellow and before frost threatens, then cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to firm the skin and develop full sweetness before storing in a cool, dry place.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center — Sweet Potato Variety List
University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Sweet Potato Varieties

common_name: Purple Passion Sweet Potato

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic sandy soil in full sun; Purple Passion is a specialty heirloom purple sweet potato distributed by small growers alongside other named purple types such as All Purple and Molokai Purple.

directions: Purple Passion is a specialty heirloom sweet potato grown as a distinct named selection within the loose group of purple-skinned, purple-fleshed sweet potatoes maintained by small seed-saving farms, producing roots with purplish skin over moderately deep purple flesh and a drier, denser texture than orange-fleshed mainstream varieties. Flavor is mildly sweet and earthy, holding its purple color best when roasted or steamed rather than boiled in acidic water, which fades the pigment. Set slips in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and keep fertility moderate, since excess nitrogen pushes vine growth at the expense of root formation; sprawling, purple-tinged vines tolerate a long, hot growing season well. Harvest after vines begin to yellow and before frost, then cure at warm temperature and high humidity for a week or two to heal skin wounds and develop full sweetness before moving roots to cool, dry storage.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center — Sweet Potato Variety List
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Sweet Potato Varieties

common_name: Supersett Crookneck Squash (Powdery Mildew Resistant Hybrid Yellow Crookneck)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Supersett is a disease-resistant hybrid yellow crookneck bred to hold foliage and production longer into the season under powdery mildew pressure than open-pollinated crookneck types.

directions: Supersett is a hybrid yellow crookneck squash bred for improved tolerance to powdery mildew, a disease that shuts down foliage and yield on older open-pollinated crookneck varieties by midsummer in humid climates. Its compact bush habit and heavy, sustained fruit set make it a productive choice for gardeners who have struggled with mildew collapse on standard crookneck squash, particularly in the humid Southeast and Gulf South where warm, humid nights favor the disease. Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; harvest young at 5-6 inches long for the best tenderness, picking every day or two during peak production since crookneck squash left on the plant quickly becomes tough and seedy and signals the plant to slow production. Scout regularly for squash vine borer and squash bugs, which affect Supersett the same as other Cucurbita pepo crooknecks despite its improved mildew tolerance.
sources: Willhite Seed Co. — Supersett Hybrid Crookneck
Louisiana State University AgCenter
University of Florida IFAS Extension

common_name: Gentry Crookneck Squash (Disease-Tolerant Hybrid Yellow Crookneck)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gentry is a modern hybrid yellow crookneck bred for disease tolerance and heavy, uniform fruit set, commonly recommended alongside 'Supersett' as a mildew-tolerant alternative to older open-pollinated crookneck varieties.

directions: Gentry is a hybrid yellow crookneck squash selected for improved disease tolerance and heavy, uniform production of smooth, warty-skinned, classically curved fruit, giving Southern gardeners a more resilient alternative to older open-pollinated crookneck lines that decline quickly once powdery mildew takes hold. The compact, open bush habit keeps fruit visible and easy to pick, and plants continue setting well through the heart of summer heat if harvested regularly. Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed; pick fruit young, at 5-6 inches, for the most tender texture and mildest flavor, checking plants daily during peak season since oversized fruit quickly turns tough, seedy, and signals the plant to slow production. As with all summer squash, consistent moisture and a thick mulch layer help maintain steady yields through hot, humid Gulf South summers.
sources: Willhite Seed Co. — Gentry Hybrid Crookneck
Louisiana State University AgCenter
University of Florida IFAS Extension

common_name: Tennessee Candy Roaster (Southern Appalachian Heritage Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills 5-6 feet apart after last frost; Tennessee Candy Roaster is a regionally distinct Appalachian candy roaster strain, similar to but selected separately from the North Georgia and Big Orange candy roaster types.

directions: Tennessee Candy Roaster is one of several closely related, regionally maintained Appalachian candy roaster strains, distinguished from the salmon-pink North Georgia type by generally more elongated, tapered fruit with tan to golden-bronze skin and less pronounced blue bloom at maturity. Like other candy roasters it carries dense, deep orange-yellow flesh with exceptionally high sugar content that concentrates further with roasting, the trait that gives the whole candy roaster group its name and its devoted following among Appalachian home gardeners and seed savers. Give the long, vigorous vines ample room to sprawl in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set to size the large fruit properly. Harvest once the rind has hardened fully and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry and cork, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry spot before moving to cool storage, where the flavor continues to improve for months.
sources: Sow True Seed — Tennessee Candy Roaster
Seed Savers Exchange — Candy Roaster squash heritage documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Appalachian heirloom squash notes

common_name: Big Orange Candy Roaster (Large Bright-Orange Appalachian Heritage Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills 5-6 feet apart after last frost, allowing generous room for very long, vigorous vines; Big Orange Candy Roaster was selected within the Appalachian candy roaster group specifically for larger fruit and a fully orange rind rather than the salmon-pink to tan skin of related strains.

directions: Big Orange Candy Roaster is an Appalachian candy roaster strain selected for larger fruit size and a solid, bright orange rind, setting it apart at a glance from the salmon-pink North Georgia type and the tan-bronze Tennessee type within the same regionally diverse candy roaster group. Fruits are elongated to slightly bulbous with a curved neck, commonly reaching 15-25 pounds or more under good growing conditions, and the thick, dense, deep-orange flesh shares the group's signature high sugar content that intensifies dramatically when roasted low and slow. Give the exceptionally long, vigorous vines plenty of room to sprawl in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with steady moisture through flowering and fruit development to size the large fruit fully. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the stem has dried and corked, then cure two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before moving to cool storage, where the flesh continues to sweeten for months.
sources: Sow True Seed — Candy Roaster squash varieties
Seed Savers Exchange — Candy Roaster squash heritage documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Appalachian heirloom squash notes
